name: Replication Best Practices
description: This module captures the best practices for replication, distilled from common failure modes and what tends to hold up over time.
content:
This module captures the best practices for replication, distilled from common failure modes and what tends to hold up over time.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Keep replication changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
2. State assumptions about replication explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
3. Prefer the simplest replication approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
4. Before starting replication work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
5. Surface known limitations of a chosen replication approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
6. Validate replication outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
7. Document any non-obvious replication decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
8. Measure before optimizing any replication bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
9. Prefer explicit, readable replication solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
10. When replication guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
11. Check that replication terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
12. Re-check edge cases relevant to replication (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not skip documenting replication assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of replication correctness.
- Avoid mixing unrelated replication concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not apply generic replication advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for replication, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
